newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians protest wage delays with strikes, marches.
newsitem.headline: Russians protest wage delays with strikes, marches.

text.p: Tens of thousands of workers marched through Russia's Pacific port city of Vladivostok on Thursday as a day of protests against unpaid pensions and wages unrolled across the world's biggest country.
The marchers -- unions said 50,000 of them, the police put the figure at 15,000 -- carried red banners and some called on the government to quit as they snaked through the city.
"I want to live without shocks and without Yeltsin's therapy," read one banner, referring to the economic reforms President Boris Yeltsin is trying to introduce in Russia.
The protest had been organised weeks in advance by trade unions and Russia's communist-led opposition, both bitter at the fact that millions of workers have not been paid for months.
"First wages, then taxes," read one banner flying above a crowd of about 1,000 in the far eastern city of Magadan, once a main clearing centre for Soviet GULag labour camps.

The day of protest appears designed to channel frustrations which have built up steadily during the six years of chaotic and crime-ridden economic transition which has opened a huge gulf between rich and poor since it began in 1992.
Ministers admit workers and pensioners are owed 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion), including 10 trillion from the state.
Under pressure from the International Monetary Fund to meet its economic promises, a new cabinet team made a priority this week of collecting taxes in order to pay its bills.

In Yeltsin's home Urals region around Yekaterinburg some 25,000 people were expected to join the strikes. The march, which started at 0700 GMT, was due to finish at the monument to Soviet state founder Vladimir Lenin in the centre of the city.
Yekaterinburg, a closed city in Soviet times, is home to a large number of defence industry firms, many of which have found it hard to cope with the tough new world of market economics.

Ministers, many appointed in a big reshuffle over the last few weeks, have promised to resolve the wage crisis as quickly as possible. But young new first deputy prime ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov have also pledged to speed up reforms.

The changes, designed to transform the Soviet-era centrally planned economy into a market system modelled on that in the West, have brought colourful goods into Russia's once-bare shops, but millions of people cannot afford to buy.
Government officials have appealed for calm, but say they have no reason to fear the situation will get out of control.
"We have the reserves to maintain public order, both troops and police, and we have taken a number of preventive measures," Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said on Wednesday.
"We sent warnings to some people about the unacceptabity of provocative actions. But we do not foresee any special difficulties," he told Russian Public Television.
Unions have forecast that 20 million will take part, but early numbers suggested they would fall short of that.
Many factories are already at a standstill and firms in the key metals and energy sectors have already said output will not be affected. Air traffic controllers do not plan to strike.
In Moscow, there was little obvious strike action early on a cold but sunny morning, and marches were only due to start in the city centre in the afternoon.

Dozens of armed OMON police commandos in riot gear lined a street south of the centre where protesters were due to gather. Several police trucks were parked close to the White House government building.
